nameStory: Eastern cottonwood gets its name from the fluffy white 'cotton' that surrounds its seeds, creating snowstorm-like drifts when released in early summer. The scientific name 'deltoides' refers to the triangular, delta-shaped leaves that are one of this tree's signature features.
description: Eastern cottonwood is a fast-growing giant among New England trees, capable of reaching 80-100 feet tall with a broad, open crown. This impressive deciduous tree has distinctive triangular leaves that shimmer and rustle in the slightest breeze, creating a constant gentle murmur. The bark starts smooth and greenish-white on young trees, developing deep furrows and ridges as it matures into a stately riverside sentinel.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Triangular leaves with flattened petioles (leaf stems) that cause them to flutter dramatically in even light breezes, creating a distinctive shimmering effect and rustling sound

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Cottony white tufts surrounding tiny seeds drift through the air in early summer like snow, often collecting in drifts against fences and buildings

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young bark is smooth and greenish-white; mature bark becomes deeply furrowed with thick, diamond-shaped ridges that feel rough and corky to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Massive tree with a broad, spreading crown and thick trunk; one of the largest deciduous trees in New England, often towering over surrounding vegetation

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Large, sticky, resinous buds in winter that smell sweet and balsamy when crushed; buds are reddish-brown and quite noticeable on bare branches

habitat: Eastern cottonwood thrives along rivers, streams, and floodplains throughout New England, preferring rich, moist soils that flood occasionally. You'll often find it growing alongside willows, silver maples, and other water-loving trees in low-lying areas. While native to western North America, it has naturalized in New England and is sometimes planted as a fast-growing shade tree.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge bright green in late spring, and drooping catkins (flower clusters) appear before the leaves are fully developed. The sticky, fragrant buds are particularly noticeable as they swell and break open.
seasonality.summer: The famous cotton-like seeds fill the air in early summer, often creating temporary 'snowstorms' that can last several days. Mature triangular leaves create the characteristic rustling sound throughout the growing season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright golden-yellow, creating spectacular fall displays, especially along waterways. The large size of the trees makes their autumn color visible from great distances.
seasonality.winter: Large, sticky buds and distinctive furrowed bark on mature trees make identification possible. The massive size and riverside location are key winter identification clues.

funFact: A single mature eastern cottonwood can release over 25 million seeds in one season, each one equipped with its own personal parachute of cottony fluff that can travel over 5 miles on the wind!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other large poplars, but eastern cottonwood's triangular leaves with flattened stems that cause extreme flutter, plus its massive size and preference for wet areas, distinguish it from quaking aspen (much smaller, whiter bark) and bigtooth aspen (leaves more oval with larger teeth).
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'eastern' cottonwood, this species is actually native to the Great Plains and western regions, but has naturalized in New England through planting and natural spread. It's part of the same family as willows and shares their love of wet places.
compareHints: Eastern cottonwood dwarfs its poplar relatives in New England - quaking aspen and bigtooth aspen rarely exceed 50 feet, while cottonwood can reach 100+ feet. Unlike the round-toothed leaves of quaking aspen or the large-toothed leaves of bigtooth aspen, cottonwood has distinctly triangular leaves. Balsam poplar has more oval leaves and is much less common in southern New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's aspens, bigtooth aspen has the largest leaf teeth - quaking aspen has tiny, fine teeth while bigtooth's are chunky and rounded.
Among New England's aspens and poplars, quaking aspen has the smallest, most finely-toothed leaves and the most constant trembling motion.
Among New England's poplars, balsam poplar is the only one with intensely fragrant buds — quaking and bigtooth aspens have smaller, less aromatic buds.

White poplar stands apart from native New England poplars by its distinctly white, woolly leaf undersides - all our native aspens and cottonwoods have smooth, pale green to silvery undersides instead.
Unlike quaking aspen with its flattened leaf stems that make leaves tremble, swamp cottonwood has round leaf stems and much larger, heart-shaped leaves.
Among New England poplars, black poplar stands out with its distinctly dark, deeply furrowed bark - much darker than Eastern cottonwood's light gray bark or the smooth bark of aspens.
